prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Definition The green partition between carriageways; the one located between the upstream and downstream motor vehicle lanes is the central median; the one located between motor vehicle lanes and non-motorized lanes or between motor vehicle lanes in the same direction is the side median. 2. Layout forms A. Central median a. The central median of urban arterial roads with a design speed higher than 60 km/h shall be densely planted with evergreen plants to avoid glare interference from oncoming traffic at night. 70 b. Within the range of 0.6 m to 1.5 m above the surface of the adjacent motor vehicle roadway, the plants configured shall have dense foliage throughout the year, and their spacing shall not be greater than 5 times the canopy spread. c. The width of the central median shall be 1.5 m or more, and a formal arrangement structure shall be adopted; simple repetition is preferable to create rhythm. At intersections and important nodes, plants shall mainly be low shrubs; planting trees is strictly prohibited to avoid tree trunks causing glare and traffic accidents. Where the width of the side green belt between carriageways is less than 1.5 m, shrubs shall be the main planting type, and shrubs and groundcover plants should be combined. 71 Figure 3.3-2 Schematic diagram of central median C. Figure 2.1-9 Layout Forms of Roadside Parking Lanes On roads with relatively heavy traffic function, on-street parking should be avoided as far as possible; in areas with weaker traffic function and greater parking demand, parallel on-street parking may be adopted. Two-way roads with a carriageway width of not less than 15 m may provide parking on both sides; two-way roads with a width of less than 10 m shall not provide parking spaces. One-way roads with a carriageway width of not less than 10 m may provide parking on one side; one-way roads with a width of less than 8 m shall not provide parking spaces. The conventional width of a roadside parking lane is 2.5 m; where conditions are constrained, the width may be appropriately reduced. 2.2 At-Grade Intersections 2.2.1 Forms and General Requirements 1. The design of at-grade intersections shall follow the following design principles: A. Where the sum of the widening section and the tapering transition section between two adjacent intersections is close to (or exceeds) the distance between the two intersections, the road section should be widened as an integrated whole. B. The channelization design of at-grade intersections shall not reduce the passage space for pedestrians and non-motorized vehicles; pedestrian passages at the convergence point of pedestrian flows at intersection corners should be appropriately widened. 2.2.2 Width of Entry/Exit Approaches and Number of Lanes 1. Traffic organization design shall follow the principles of separation of pedestrians and vehicles, separation of motorized and non-motorized traffic, and travel in designated lanes; people-centered design and bus priority; safety and smooth flow, with reduced delay. The conditions for setting dedicated turning lanes are as follows: where the average arrival volume of right-turning vehicles per signal cycle reaches 4 vehicles within the peak 15 minutes, or where space permits, a dedicated right-turn lane shall be provided. 2. The layout of intersection approach roads shall meet the following requirements: at intersections between arterial roads and secondary arterial roads, the number of through lanes on the approach road (including through-left or through-right lanes) shall not be less than the number of lanes on the road section. 3. The lanes on the exit road of an intersection shall match the maximum number of approach lanes flowing into the same signal phase from the upstream approaches. For reconstructed intersections with constrained conditions, the maximum number of inflow approach lanes may be reduced by one. Figure 2.1-3 Tidal Lane and Movable Barrier 2.1.3 Shared Lane 1. The design concept of shared roads emphasizes the integration of sidewalk and motor vehicle lane space. The use of shared-road space is pedestrian-oriented. In terms of functional space, it meets the different needs of different groups, including walking, cycling, and motor vehicles. In terms of planning concept, shared roads emphasize people-centered design, serving pedestrians and providing convenience for urban residents, making them more willing to gather in shared-road spaces. Figure 2.1-4 Street View of a Shared Road 2. The entire cross-section of a shared road is divided into a sidewalk and a shared carriageway. The sidewalk is exclusively for pedestrians and is integrated with the building frontage area. The shared carriageway is for all travelers; pedestrians, motor vehicles, and non-motorized vehicles may all travel on the shared carriageway. 3. A “time-limited pedestrian street” form may also be adopted, whereby motor vehicle access is prohibited during specified periods on part of the road, and a high-quality block combining commerce and culture is created in conjunction with the characteristics of the road section. 2.1.4 Median The median shall be enclosed with curb stones. Where anti-collision requirements need to be considered, anti-collision guardrails of the corresponding grade shall be used. When rainwater detention facilities need to be installed in the road median, the curb stone arrangement shall meet drainage requirements. 2.1.5 Bus-Only Lane 1. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 3 lanes or more (including 3 lanes), or the total one-way motor vehicle roadway width is not less than 11 m; where one-way passenger bus volume on the road section exceeds 6,000 persons/peak hour, or bus flow exceeds 150 vehicles/peak hour; and where the average section flow per lane exceeds 500 vehicles/peak hour. 2. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 4 lanes or more (including 4 lanes), and the one-way bus flow on the section exceeds 90 vehicles/peak hour. 3. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 2 lanes, the one-way passenger bus volume exceeds 6,000 persons/peak hour, and bus flow exceeds 150 vehicles/peak hour. 29 4. After paving, the lane color is conspicuous and forms a sharp contrast with the adjacent ordinary motor vehicle lane, preventing ordinary motor vehicles from mistakenly entering the lane. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)

All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort

- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

Facility requirements: • Provide convenient and safe pedestrian crossings; for life-service roads of higher grade, encourage elevated pedestrian crossings, curb extensions, and other traffic-calming facilities, and speed limits. • Encourage the use of green forms such as lawns, sparse tree stands, rows of trees, shrubs, and planting of trees and other vegetation to create a people-oriented, green environment. • Consider larger-canopy trees; for tall planting, the root space should be relatively small to ensure pedestrian passage space. • Use non-open interfaces on both sides as the main form; road greenery may be used to create transparent, screened, separated, and other visual-control effects. 9 Landscape-recreation roads Recommendations for upgrading and improving interface types General requirements: • Encourage the integration of urban landscape and recreational functions, balancing landscape and leisure activities with residents’ daily travel needs. • Increase the amount of green space along the line to avoid vegetation becoming an obstacle to activities. Spatial requirements: • Roads of this type should combine waterfront space and roadside green space, and use connected green spaces and widened building setbacks to create street-side open spaces. • In areas with abundant road space, pedestrian and bicycle lanes or dedicated motor-vehicle and non-motorized lanes may be set up, with public facilities arranged on one side. • Encourage the use of “sea-sponge city” technology, using side ditches, median strips, and roadside green belts, as well as smart rainwater-management facilities, to shape block-like or belt-like forms and to regulate and purify rainwater. Facility requirements: • Use vegetation to shape different forms, emphasizing seasonal changes, increasing landscape layering, and enhancing road recognizability. • Select ornamental trees, flowers, and other plants, and arrange them in combination to strengthen the road’s distinctive character. • Encourage the setting of slow-mobility facilities such

Definition The green partition between carriageways; the one located between the upstream and downstream motor vehicle lanes is the central median; the one located between motor vehicle lanes and non-motorized lanes or between motor vehicle lanes in the same direction is the side median. 2. Layout forms A. Central median a. The central median of urban arterial roads with a design speed higher than 60 km/h shall be densely planted with evergreen plants to avoid glare interference from oncoming traffic at night. 70 b. Within the range of 0.6 m to 1.5 m above the surface of the adjacent motor vehicle roadway, the plants configured shall have dense foliage throughout the year, and their spacing shall not be greater than 5 times the canopy spread. c. The width of the central median shall be 1.5 m or more, and a formal arrangement structure shall be adopted; simple repetition is preferable to create rhythm. At intersections and important nodes, plants shall mainly be low shrubs; planting trees is strictly prohibited to avoid tree trunks causing glare and traffic accidents. Two-way roads with a carriageway width of not less than 15 m may provide parking on both sides; two-way roads with a width of less than 10 m shall not provide parking spaces. The conventional width of a roadside parking lane is 2.5 m; where conditions are constrained, the width may be appropriately reduced. 2.2 At-Grade Intersections 2.2.1 Forms and General Requirements 1. The design of at-grade intersections shall follow the following design principles: A. Where the sum of the widening section and the tapering transition section between two adjacent intersections is close to (or exceeds) the distance between the two intersections, the road section should be widened as an integrated whole. B. The channelization design of at-grade intersections shall not reduce the passage space for pedestrians and non-motorized vehicles; pedestrian passages at the convergence point of pedestrian flows at intersection corners should be appropriately widened. 2.2.2 Width of Entry/Exit Approaches and Number of Lanes 1. Traffic organization design shall follow the principles of separation of pedestrians and vehicles, separation of motorized and non-motorized traffic, and travel in designated lanes; people-centered design and bus priority; safety and smooth flow, with reduced delay. The conditions for setting dedicated turning lanes are as follows: where the average arrival volume of right-turning vehicles per signal cycle reaches 4 vehicles within the peak 15 minutes, or where space permits, a dedicated right-turn lane shall be provided. 2. The layout of intersection approach roads shall meet the following requirements: at intersections between arterial roads and secondary arterial roads, the number of through lanes on the approach road (including through-left or through-right lanes) shall not be less than the number of lanes on the road section. 3. The lanes on the exit road of an intersection shall match the maximum number of approach lanes flowing into the same signal phase from the upstream approaches. For reconstructed intersections with constrained conditions, the maximum number of inflow approach lanes may be reduced by one. Where adjacent approaches are provided with dedicated right-turn lanes, the exit road shall be widened by one dedicated right-turn exit

Facility requirements: • Increase slow-mobility signage and pedestrian wayfinding signage to strengthen walkability. • Roadside municipal facilities such as traffic poles, lamp posts, and trash bins should be arranged in a rational manner to preserve the historic and cultural character of the streets and lanes. 12 Comprehensive roads Recommendations for upgrading and improving interface types General requirements: • Comprehensive roads are roads that combine multiple road-type characteristics, with a relatively high degree of mixing between road functions and interface types, and may include roads with commercial and service functions as well as urban traffic functions. For comprehensive roads, the street design should be targeted according to the requirements of multiple road-type characteristics. Facility requirements: • Provide continuous facilities, and arrange trees, leisure seating, outdoor display areas, self-parking spaces, roadside temporary parking, and roadside greenery in an integrated manner to facilitate residents’ daily activities. 13 Introduction 1. Purpose of Formulation Under the macro guidance of the “General Provisions,” these Detailed Rules aim at the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads, and are expanded and implemented from four directions: human-oriented, quality-oriented, distinctive, and intelligent. They interpret the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads in the form of colorful labels, and create urban colorful roads unique to Suzhou. ➢ Human-oriented: Starting from the users of Suzhou’s urban roads, and taking the public’s experience of urban road space as the benchmark, fully consider the comfort, safety, and convenience of public activities, and realize the value shift from “vehicle-centered” to “people-centered.” ➢ Quality-oriented: Vigorously improve the travel quality of people and vehicle traffic in Suzhou, and emphasize the public space function of roads. Appropriately raise the standards for urban road design, construction, and maintenance, extend road service life, and improve users’ comfort of experience. Reflect a road construction level of high appearance and high standards, with attention to detail and control. ➢ Distinctive: Adapt measures to local conditions, and through the embedding of Suzhou-style elements and the creation of road characteristic scenes, highlight Suzhou’s distinctive urban character of integration between tradition and modernity, so that urban roads become an important carrier and display space for the “Jiangnan culture” brand, and continue the city’s historical and cultural lineage. ➢ Intelligent: Deploy intelligent sensing devices along the roadside, together with cloud service platforms, computing and communication facilities, and through data technologies such as autonomous driving and vehicle-road coordination, realize a travel experience of deep interaction among people, vehicles, and road space, assist safe driving and autonomous driving, and create demonstration roads with Suzhou’s smart-city characteristics. 2. Figure 2.1-3 Tidal Lane and Movable Barrier 2.1.3 Shared Lane 1. The design concept of shared roads emphasizes the integration of sidewalk and motor vehicle lane space. The use of shared-road space is pedestrian-oriented. In terms of functional space, it meets the different needs of different groups, including walking, cycling, and motor vehicles. In terms of planning concept, shared roads emphasize people-centered design, serving pedestrians and providing convenience for urban residents, making them more willing to gather in shared-road spaces. Figure 2.1-4 Street View of a Shared Road 2. The entire cross-section of a shared road is divided into a sidewalk and a shared carriageway. The sidewalk is exclusively for pedestrians and is integrated with the building frontage area. The shared carriageway is for all travelers; pedestrians, motor vehicles, and non-motorized vehicles may all travel on the shared carriageway. 3. A “time-limited pedestrian street” form may also be adopted, whereby motor vehicle access is prohibited during specified periods on part of the road, and a high-quality block combining commerce and culture is created in conjunction with the characteristics of the road section. 2.1.4 Median The median shall be enclosed with curb stones. Where anti-collision requirements need to be considered, anti-collision guardrails of the corresponding grade shall be used. When rainwater detention facilities need to be installed in the road median, the curb stone arrangement shall meet drainage requirements. 2.1.5 Bus-Only Lane 1. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 3 lanes or more (including 3 lanes), or the total one-way motor vehicle roadway width is not less than 11 m; where one-way passenger bus volume on the road section exceeds 6,000 persons/peak hour, or bus flow exceeds 150 vehicles/peak hour; and where the average section flow per lane exceeds 500 vehicles/peak hour. 2. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 4 lanes or more (including 4 lanes), and the one-way bus flow on the section exceeds 90 vehicles/peak hour. 3. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 2 lanes, the one-way passenger bus volume exceeds 6,000 persons/peak hour, and bus flow exceeds 150 vehicles/peak hour. 29 4. Bus-only lanes may be paved with colored asphalt. After paving, the lane color is conspicuous and forms a sharp contrast with the adjacent ordinary motor vehicle lane, preventing ordinary motor vehicles from mistakenly entering the lane.
